title: Why One Neighborhood Collapses While the Next Stays Standing
description: Why earthquake shaking varies street by street: surface waves, soft soil, sedimentary basins, resonance, rupture direction and ridges, from Loma Prieta to Bangkok.
dek: One earthquake has one magnitude, yet one site can shake ten times harder than its neighbor. Here is how surface waves, soft ground, basins and building height decide where the damage falls.
cardImage: the app's seismic wave widget on the Surface tab: a grid of particles moving in a rolling wave along the direction of travel

sections.h: One Earthquake, Many Outcomes
p: An earthquake has a single magnitude and a single epicenter, yet it produces a wide range of shaking across the region around it. The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) explains that shaking at any site depends on the distance from the earthquake, on the rock and soil beneath the site, and on complexities in how seismic waves travel through the crust (USGS n.d.a). The Southern California Earthquake Center (SCEC) reports that in a single earthquake the shaking at one site can easily be ten times stronger than at a neighboring site, even when both lie the same distance from the ruptured fault (SCEC n.d.).

That variation accounts for the uneven damage seen after large earthquakes. A district of collapsed apartment blocks can lie a short distance from a district where chimneys remain intact. The cause usually involves the ground beneath each block, the way waves travelling along the surface interact with that ground, and the design of the buildings themselves. The sections below follow the waves from the fault to the foundation.

sections.h: Waves That Travel Along the Surface
p: Earthquakes radiate two families of waves. Body waves, the P and S waves, pass through the planet's interior. Surface waves form where that energy reaches the top of the crust, and they travel along the ground surface. Love waves move the ground horizontally, side to side, and Rayleigh waves move it in a rolling, elliptical motion. Surface waves arrive after the S waves and fade with distance more gradually than body waves do, so they often produce the strongest and longest shaking far from the fault.

A USGS computer simulation of a magnitude 6.5 earthquake on the Seattle Fault illustrates the sequence. The later pulses that follow the initial S wave are surface-wave energy, and they dominate the long-period motion across the northern part of the simulated area (USGS n.d.b). Joyner (2000) analyzed the strong motion produced by surface waves in deep sedimentary basins, which are the settings where this energy matters most.

sections.h: Soft Ground Amplifies Shaking
p: The first local control on damage is the stiffness of the ground. SCEC identifies two geologic factors as most important in southern California: the softness of the rock or soil near the surface and the total thickness of the sediments above hard bedrock (SCEC n.d.). Hazard models represent softness with a single number, Vs30, the average shear-wave velocity in the top 30 meters of ground. Gallahue et al. (2022) report that at the long periods of 1 to 5 seconds that affect tall buildings, these site terms raise mapped hazard by factors of 1 to 3 at many sites, relative to a standard reference condition of firm rock with a Vs30 of 760 meters per second.

The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake gave a clear example. Soft soils amplified the strong shaking by a factor of about two and caused damage at distances up to 100 kilometers from the epicenter (Holzer 1992). In San Francisco's Marina District, which was built on a cove filled in gradually from the late 1860s to 1912, most of the settlement, liquefaction, and damage to pipelines and foundations occurred in areas of artificial fill (Bonilla 1991). Liquefaction, in which saturated sandy ground temporarily loses its strength, occurred at 134 locations during the earthquake and accounted for $99.2 million of the total loss of $5.9 billion (Holzer 1992). Liquefaction therefore concentrated damage in specific places, and most of the loss came from other causes.

Amplification has limits. Gallahue et al. (2022) note that nonlinear deamplification grows as shaking intensifies and, for very strong shaking, can overcome the linear amplification. Soft soil therefore raises shaking in moderate events and can reduce it in the strongest ones.

sections.h: Basins Trap and Prolong the Waves
p: Thick sediment layers in a basin act as a container for surface waves. In the Seattle simulation, surface waves are trapped by the relatively unconsolidated deposits within roughly the top 2 kilometers of the basin, and long-period shaking in Seattle lasts about 25 seconds (USGS n.d.b). The result is higher amplitude and longer duration than a rock site at the same distance would experience.

The 2015 Gorkha earthquake in Nepal produced a measured example in the Kathmandu Valley. Recordings at sedimentary sites showed long-duration, long-period oscillations attributed to the valley response, with horizontal amplification of about 10 (Takai et al. 2016). The predominant period and the envelope of the oscillations differed from site to site, which the authors read as evidence of a complicated basin structure. Their velocity response spectra indicated enough destructive power to damage high-rise buildings with natural periods of 3 to 5 seconds (Takai et al. 2016).

sections.h: When Ground and Building Vibrate Together
p: Every structure has a natural period, the time it takes to sway through one full cycle, and taller buildings generally have longer periods. When ground motion repeats at a period close to a building's own, each cycle adds to the last and the response grows. This is resonance.

Mexico City in 1985 is the standard case. The earthquake struck more than 350 kilometers away (Dalziel and Nassirpour 2025). Martinez-Romero (1987) reports peak accelerations of 0.15 g in the epicentral area and between 0.01 g and 0.19 g in Mexico City, depending on the ground conditions at each site. Ground motion in the damage area had a period of about 2 seconds, at least twenty strong cycles were recorded, and strong shaking lasted roughly one minute. Martinez-Romero attributes these long-period motions to the unique subsoil of the lake bed zone and estimates that about 400 buildings collapsed. Suzuki and Kiremidjian (1986) found that reinforced concrete frame buildings of 6 to 15 stories accounted for most of the damage in the soft-soil area, and they describe the long period and long duration, about three minutes, as the defining characteristics of the ground motion.

The match between building height and ground period is a simplification, because stiffness, condition, and construction quality all alter a building's actual period and strength. Resonance accounts for the pattern of damage by height, and engineers treat it as one factor among several.

sections.h: Distance Offers Less Protection Than Expected
p: The Mw 7.7 Mandalay earthquake in Myanmar on 28 March 2025 extended the same lesson to a far greater range. More than 1,000 kilometers away in Bangkok, a 30-story tower under construction collapsed, with at least 96 fatalities (Dalziel and Nassirpour 2025). A New Zealand reconnaissance team that examined ten Bangkok buildings reported that the earthquake produced widespread shaking in a deep sedimentary basin, and that non-structural elements such as infill walls, ceilings, and facade components sustained the most widespread damage (naturalhazards.govt.nz 2026).

The 2011 Tohoku earthquake produced a related effect. Long-period waves traveled more than 370 kilometers and caused high-rise buildings in Tokyo and Osaka to sway for minutes, with non-structural damage (Dalziel and Nassirpour 2025). Long periods decay slowly and match the natural periods of tall buildings, so the hazard to those buildings can extend well beyond the distances that damage low-rise construction.

sections.h: Rupture Direction and Local Topography
p: Harold Tobin, director of the Pacific Northwest Seismic Network, names basin effects and rupture direction as two major complications beyond simple distance (KING 5 n.d.). When a fault rupture travels toward a site, energy from successive parts of the fault arrives together and concentrates into a strong pulse. A site on the far side of the rupture receives a weaker, longer signal. Two towns at equal distance from the epicenter can therefore receive different shaking.

Ridges and hilltops add another possible contribution. After the 2010 Haiti earthquake, unusually severe damage occurred near Hotel Montana on a ridge in Petionville. Hough et al. (2010) concluded that poor construction was primarily responsible for the extent of damage in Haiti, but that topographic amplification contributed significantly in Petionville. Their aftershock recordings showed ground motion on the ridge amplified relative to adjacent valley stations and to a hard-rock reference site, which sediment amplification alone could not explain.

sections.h: Where Scientists Disagree
p: The Petionville case remains contested. Assimaki and Jeong (2013) tested topography against soil conditions. Their simulations showed that neither the shape of the ridge alone nor the soil alone explained the recordings, while a model with a layer of soft soil over bedrock beneath the ridge matched them well. They concluded that the recorded amplification is most likely attributable to coupled site and topographic effects. Whether a given hill adds shaking through its relief, through its layered soil, or through both varies from case to case.

The Marina District evidence contains a related ambiguity. Bonilla (1991) notes that recordings and building damage in 1989 indicate amplified motion on both natural and artificial ground, which suggests that the bedrock surface and the thickness of the clay and sand deposits beneath the fill influenced the shaking. Ground failure, by contrast, concentrated in the fill.

sections.h: How Engineers Use the Pattern
p: Mapping site conditions turns these findings into practical tools. SCEC combined surface softness with sediment thickness to predict where amplification will be highest, and it identifies the areas of greatest expected amplification as hotspots (SCEC n.d.). USGS ShakeMap, posted normally within several minutes of a moderate or large earthquake, shows ground shaking itself and not the source parameters of magnitude and epicenter (USGS n.d.a). The reported magnitude and epicenter describe the source of an earthquake. The ground beneath a given street, together with the buildings on it, determines what that street experiences.

faq.q: Why can shaking differ so much between neighborhoods in the same earthquake?
faq.a: Shaking at a site depends on its distance from the earthquake, the rock and soil beneath it, and how seismic waves travel through the crust. The Southern California Earthquake Center reports that one site can shake about ten times more strongly than a neighboring site at the same distance from the fault.

faq.q: What are surface waves?
faq.a: Surface waves form when earthquake energy reaches the top of the crust and travels along the ground. Love waves move the ground side to side, and Rayleigh waves move it in a rolling motion. They arrive after the P and S waves and fade more slowly with distance, so they often cause the strongest and longest shaking far from the fault.

faq.q: Does soft ground always make shaking worse?
faq.a: Usually, but not always. Soft soil and thick sediments amplify moderate shaking; in the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake soft soils roughly doubled it. In very strong shaking, soft soil behaves nonlinearly and can reduce the shaking instead.

faq.q: Why did buildings in Mexico City collapse in 1985 so far from the earthquake?
faq.a: The old lake bed under Mexico City shook at a period of about 2 seconds for a long time. Buildings of roughly 6 to 15 stories have natural periods close to that, so they resonated, and reinforced concrete frames of that height accounted for most of the damage in the soft-soil zone.

faq.q: Can an earthquake damage buildings more than 1,000 kilometers away?
faq.a: Yes. The Mw 7.7 Mandalay earthquake in Myanmar in 2025 brought down a 30-story tower under construction in Bangkok, more than 1,000 kilometers away. Long-period waves decay slowly with distance, and Bangkok sits on a deep sedimentary basin.

faq.q: What does ShakeMap show?
faq.a: USGS ShakeMap shows how strongly the ground shook across a region, rather than only the magnitude and epicenter. It is normally posted within several minutes of a moderate or large earthquake.

title: From Richter to Moment Magnitude: Why the Number Changes After an Earthquake
description: Why earthquake magnitudes are revised: Richter's local scale, saturation, moment magnitude, W phase and the Tohoku 7.9-to-9.0 update, and why agencies differ.
dek: The first magnitude is a fast estimate, and it is meant to change. Here is how Richter's scale gave way to moment magnitude, and what each revision tells you.
cardImage: the app's magnitude widget at M6.0, with circles for M4.0, M5.0 and M6.0 whose areas show the energy released (each step about 32 times more), an estimated energy of about 15 kilotons of TNT and about 158 such earthquakes a year worldwide

sections.h: The Number Behind the Headline
p: Within minutes of a significant earthquake, one number appears on phones, news feeds, and tracking sites: the magnitude. An hour later it may read differently, and a few days later it may change again. These revisions often prompt the question of whether seismologists made an error. In most cases the revision reflects a planned sequence of estimates, in which the first figure is a fast calculation from the earliest data and later figures use more data and a better-suited method.

Magnitude scales are logarithmic. According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), a ten-fold drop in wave amplitude lowers the magnitude by one unit (USGS n.d.a). Each unit also corresponds to about 32 times more energy released (USGS n.d.e). A change of 0.1 or 0.2 therefore has a small physical meaning, while a change of a full unit or more indicates that the first estimate described a very different earthquake.

The popular name for the scale, the Richter scale, remains in everyday use even though most agencies no longer rely on it for large events. The USGS describes Richter magnitude as a well-known but poorly understood concept (USGS n.d.a). The history of how it was replaced explains most of what happens after an earthquake.

sections.h: What Richter Built in 1935
p: Charles Richter developed the first logarithmic magnitude scale in the 1930s to measure earthquakes in southern California, using relatively high-frequency data from nearby seismograph stations. The scale was labeled ML, with the L standing for local, and this is the quantity that became known as the Richter magnitude (USGS n.d.a).

ML works by reading the maximum shaking amplitude recorded at a station and correcting for the distance to the source. Each station gives its own estimate, and an average across stations produces the reported value (Gardine 2019). The method suited its original setting: a dense regional network, moderate earthquakes, and short distances. Modern seismologists still compute it. The Alaska Earthquake Center reports that its local magnitude works well, with the caveat that it applies only to events below about magnitude 6 (Gardine 2019).

sections.h: Why Larger Earthquakes Outgrew the Method
p: As more seismograph stations were installed around the world, it became apparent that Richter's procedure was strictly valid only for certain frequency and distance ranges (USGS n.d.a). Seismologists extended the idea to body-wave magnitude (mb) and surface-wave magnitude (Ms), each valid for a particular frequency range and type of seismic signal. In its range of validity, each is equivalent to the Richter magnitude (USGS n.d.a).

All three scales share a deeper limitation, which Hanks and Kanamori (1979) described as saturation. They argued that ML, Ms, and mb saturate for the same physical reason: for large enough earthquakes, these narrow-band amplitude measurements stop measuring the overall faulting process and register only a limited part of the signal. The practical result was visible in the catalogs of the time, where the maximum reported mb was about 7 and the maximum reported Ms about 8.3 (Hanks and Kanamori 1979).

In simplified terms, a great earthquake radiates energy across a wide range of frequencies, but an amplitude measured in one frequency band records only part of that signal. Two earthquakes of very different size can then produce similar amplitudes on the chosen instrument. The measurement reaches a ceiling while the earthquake keeps growing.

sections.h: Moment Magnitude: A Measure of the Source
p: Hanks and Kanamori (1979) proposed a scale built on the seismic moment, a physical property of the source that does not depend on the frequency band of an instrument. The USGS describes seismic moment as proportional to the fault slip multiplied by the area of fault surface that slips, and as related to the total energy released (USGS n.d.a). Seismologists can estimate it from seismograms or from geodetic measurements and convert it to a magnitude with a standard formula.

The formula in the 1979 paper is M = (2/3) log M0 minus 10.7, with the seismic moment M0 in dyne-centimeters. The constants were chosen so that the new scale agrees with the older ones where they were reliable. The authors reported that the relations are uniformly valid for ML between 3 and 7, for Ms between 5 and 7.5, and for moment magnitude of 7.5 and above (Hanks and Kanamori 1979). Moment magnitude (Mw) therefore matches Richter's numbers for moderate earthquakes and continues to grow with the largest ones. The USGS states that it is valid over the complete range of magnitudes, which the older scales lacked (USGS n.d.a).

Agencies apply this in practice by switching scales with size. The Alaska Earthquake Center computes a local magnitude for all earthquakes, and uses moment magnitude as soon as it is available for events of about magnitude 5.5 and above, and always for events of 6.5 or greater. It considers Mw the best current measure because it reflects the energy released directly (Gardine 2019).

sections.h: Why the First Number Is Provisional
p: The speed of the first report limits its accuracy. For large earthquakes outside the United States, the USGS releases an initial magnitude and location within about 20 minutes, using real-time data from the nearest seismic stations (USGS n.d.b). Some of the seismic waves used in magnitude analysis take more than an hour to travel around the Earth to distant stations, so that energy cannot be included in the first release. Some data from contributing networks arrive several minutes late, and some arrive days afterward (USGS n.d.b).

The USGS identifies two typical update points. The first comes within a few hours, when most real-time data have reached stations worldwide and more sophisticated processing is complete. The second comes within days to weeks, when the event is reanalyzed for the archival catalog using most available seismograms and magnitude estimates from other agencies. In California, Utah, Alaska, and the Pacific Northwest, updates can occur within minutes, particularly when a rapid magnitude is released without human review (USGS n.d.b).

Two further causes appear in routine practice. The first is a change in magnitude type. The Alaska Earthquake Center explains that its first value is usually a local magnitude, and that a larger event later receives a moment magnitude (Gardine 2019). The second is analyst review. An analyst computes a distance-weighted average across stations and can remove stations whose values differ notably from the average. Location errors matter because distance drives the calculation. An automated depth of 100 kilometers, where the true depth is 5 kilometers, makes every station appear farther away and inflates the magnitude (Gardine 2019). In one example from the center, the magnitude rose from 4.77 using 5 stations to 5.01 using 90 stations (Gardine 2019).

sections.h: The Tohoku Earthquake: A Case Study in Saturation
p: The 11 March 2011 Tohoku earthquake in Japan is the most studied example. The Japan Meteorological Agency first announced a magnitude of 7.9, and the USGS initially announced the same value (Guilhem et al. 2013). The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center's first bulletin also gave 7.9, and the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre's rapid determination yielded 8.0 (Duputel et al. 2011). Guilhem et al. (2013) attribute such underestimates to saturation: for events of this size, measurements at frequencies above the corner frequency of the rupture cannot register the full seismic moment.

The correction came from a different type of signal. W phase inversion uses a low-frequency seismic signal to estimate the moment tensor, and with it the seismic moment. Duputel et al. (2011) report that the first W phase results at the USGS and the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center gave moment magnitudes between 8.8 and 9.0. Within the hour, as more data became available, the solutions converged on a common result of about 9.0. Guilhem et al. (2013) describe a moment tensor method that determined the moment magnitude within 8 minutes of the origin time.

The Incorporated Research Institutions for Seismology (IRIS) describes the same sequence as three steps: a first estimate of 7.9 from limited data within minutes, an intermediate revision as waves reached distant stations, and a final analysis using very low frequency recordings from many stations that raised the estimate to 9.0. After that point the value in the USGS catalog generally remains fixed (IRIS n.d.). Since magnitudes are logarithmic, the step from 7.9 to 9.0 corresponds to about 45 times more energy by the same approximation noted earlier.

sections.h: Revisions in the Other Direction
p: Revisions do not always raise the number. After the 22 November 2016 earthquake in Japan, the Japan Meteorological Agency first reported a magnitude of 7.3 and later revised it to 7.4. The USGS also first reported 7.3 and later revised it down to 6.9 (AIR Worldwide 2016). The catastrophe-modeling firm that documented the case explains the difference as a product of the amount of data involved and of the continuing analysis that follows an event.

Small changes also occur long after the first week. The USGS updated the 2011 Prague, Oklahoma earthquake from Mw 5.6 to 5.7 when a re-analysis was prompted by questions about its size relative to the 2016 Pawnee earthquake. Gavin Hayes of the USGS said the difference in size between the two events is less than 0.1 magnitude units (USGS n.d.d). In Alaska, the 30 November 2018 earthquake moved from 7.0 to 7.1 after three months of review by multiple agencies and academic groups. State seismologist Michael West wrote that most of the data tilted toward 7.1, and seismologist Natalia Ruppert attributed the change to differences in how institutions measure earthquakes (Anchorage Daily News 2019).

sections.h: Where Agencies Differ
p: Two agencies can publish different magnitudes for the same earthquake, and both can be correct for their method. The USGS National Earthquake Information Center routinely calculates as many as a dozen magnitude types, because no single method accurately estimates the size of all earthquakes. Different techniques often measure different physical processes, and the USGS acknowledges that discrepancies between magnitude types for the same event can be large (USGS n.d.c).

No single scale settles every case. Mw is regarded as the best general measure (Gardine 2019). A local magnitude from a regional network and a moment magnitude from global stations answer slightly different questions. In the Oklahoma example above, the revision was a single tenth of a magnitude unit, and the USGS described the two events it compared as differing in size by less than that (USGS n.d.d).

sections.h: Reading the Number
p: A revised magnitude does not imply that the earthquake did less or more damage than first thought. IRIS notes that large earthquakes are often a cascading sequence of breaks along a long fault rupture, which complicates the first estimate (IRIS n.d.). Magnitude describes the size of the source. The shaking at a particular location also depends on distance, depth, and the local ground.

For a reader following an evolving event, the sequence is predictable. The first figure is a fast estimate, often a local magnitude. For large events a moment magnitude follows within the first hour as long-period data arrive, and the catalog value can still change slightly over the following days. A shift of a tenth or two reflects added stations and review. A shift of a full unit or more, as in the Tohoku case, reflects a change in the method used to measure the largest earthquakes.

faq.q: Why does an earthquake's magnitude change after the first report?
faq.a: The first figure is a fast estimate from the nearest stations, often a local magnitude. As seismic waves reach more distant stations and analysts review the data, agencies refine the value, and for large earthquakes they switch to moment magnitude, which describes the size of the source more completely.

faq.q: Is the Richter scale still used?
faq.a: Local magnitude, the scale Charles Richter developed in the 1930s, is still calculated by regional networks for earthquakes below about magnitude 6. For larger earthquakes agencies use moment magnitude (Mw), because Richter's method and the scales that extended it stop growing for the biggest events.

faq.q: What is moment magnitude?
faq.a: Moment magnitude, proposed by Thomas Hanks and Hiroo Kanamori in 1979, is calculated from the seismic moment, which depends on how far the fault slipped and over what area. It matches the older scales for moderate earthquakes and keeps growing for the largest ones.

faq.q: What does magnitude saturation mean?
faq.a: Older scales measure wave amplitude in a narrow frequency band. For very large earthquakes that band captures only part of the signal, so the measured value reaches a ceiling: in the catalogs Hanks and Kanamori examined, body-wave magnitudes topped out near 7 and surface-wave magnitudes near 8.3.

faq.q: Why was the 2011 Tohoku earthquake first reported as magnitude 7.9?
faq.a: The first estimates used methods that saturate for very large earthquakes. Within the hour, W phase inversions using long-period waves gave moment magnitudes of 8.8 to 9.0 and converged on about 9.0.

faq.q: Why do two agencies sometimes report different magnitudes?
faq.a: They may use different magnitude types, stations and amounts of data. The USGS calculates as many as a dozen magnitude types because no single method suits every earthquake, and discrepancies between types for the same event can be large.

title: How Earthquakes Happen 600 Kilometers Down: The Puzzle of Deep-Focus Seismicity
description: Why earthquakes 300 to 700 km deep should not happen, the 1994 Bolivia and 2013 Okhotsk events, and three mechanisms: phase change, water and runaway heating.
dek: Rock at 600 kilometers is under enormous pressure and should flow, not break. Yet large earthquakes start there. Here is what the two biggest deep events revealed and why no single explanation fits.
cardImage: a cross-section of a convergent plate boundary: an oceanic plate sinks beneath a continental plate, with earthquakes tracing the slab down to about 700 km

sections.h: Earthquakes Below the Brittle Zone
p: Most earthquakes begin within a few tens of kilometers of the surface, where cold rock breaks and slides along faults. A small share begins far deeper, inside oceanic plates that are sinking into the mantle. Earthquakes below about 70 kilometers are often grouped together as deep events (Wang et al. 2017). Within subducting plates, events shallower than 300 kilometers are defined as intermediate-depth earthquakes, and those deeper than 300 kilometers are considered deep-focus earthquakes (Hasegawa and Nakajima 2017). sisma.io uses the same boundaries in its depth labels: shallow above 70 kilometers, intermediate from 70 to 300, and deep below 300.

The deepest population occurs between about 325 and 690 kilometers, an interval that closely brackets the mantle transition zone, where the main minerals of the upper mantle change to denser crystal structures (Kirby et al. 1996). The existence of these earthquakes poses a problem. Green and Burnley (1989) point out that brittle fracture and frictional sliding at depths greater than 100 to 200 kilometers would require unrealistic rock strengths. Hasegawa and Nakajima (2017) put the difficulty in terms of stress: an earthquake at such depths would need shear stress to exceed a very large frictional strength, yet the earthquakes do occur, so some special mechanism must lower the strength of the fault. Several plausible mechanisms have been proposed, and the exact one remains unresolved (Hasegawa and Nakajima 2017).

sections.h: Where Deep Earthquakes Occur and How They Behave
p: Deep earthquakes occur in subducting or previously subducted oceanic lithosphere (Kirby et al. 1996). They follow dipping planar bands known as Wadati-Benioff zones, which trace the cold, down-going cores of the sinking plates (Wang et al. 2017). The number of earthquakes falls almost exponentially with depth to about 300 kilometers, reaches a minimum between about 300 and 450 kilometers, and rises again to a local maximum at 550 to 600 kilometers (Hasegawa and Nakajima 2017). Activity then ends abruptly near 700 kilometers (Wang et al. 2017).

Zhan (2020) summarizes the observations in a review: deep earthquakes behave like shallow earthquakes but must have fundamentally different physical processes, and their rupture behavior, size statistics and aftershocks are diverse and depend imperfectly on factors such as slab temperature, depth and magnitude. Deep events generally produce few aftershocks and leave no surface rupture or geodetic signal, which makes the size of their ruptures hard to estimate (Zhan et al. 2014).

For readers who follow earthquakes, the practical consequence is that deep earthquakes usually do not cause enough shaking at the surface to be hazardous, although they are of great scientific interest (University of California, Santa Cruz 2013). A deep event of magnitude 6 or 7 can therefore appear on a tracking site as a large number with little or no reported damage, because the rupture lies hundreds of kilometers below the ground.

sections.h: Two Record-Setting Events
p: Two earthquakes anchor most discussion. On 9 June 1994, a deep earthquake struck beneath Bolivia. Silver et al. (1995) give its moment magnitude as 8.3 and its depth as 636 kilometers, and describe it as the largest deep-focus earthquake recorded up to that time. The USGS catalog lists the same event as magnitude 8.2 at a depth of 631 kilometers (USGS n.d.a). On 24 May 2013, a magnitude 8.3 earthquake ruptured a 180-kilometer-long fault within the subducting Pacific plate about 609 kilometers below the Sea of Okhotsk (Ye et al. 2013). The USGS catalog lists it as magnitude 8.3 at 598 kilometers (USGS n.d.b). Different methods give depths that differ by several kilometers, so published figures vary slightly.

The Okhotsk earthquake had a seismic moment 30 percent larger than that of the Bolivia event and released about three times as much energy (University of California, Santa Cruz 2013). Ye et al. (2013) measured a rupture velocity of about 4.0 to 4.5 kilometers per second and a static stress drop of about 12 to 15 megapascals, values compatible with theoretical radiation efficiency for crack models. A nearby aftershock had a stress drop one to two orders of magnitude higher, which the authors read as large stress heterogeneity in the deep slab. Thorne Lay, a coauthor of the study, called it a mystery how rock can slide against rock so fast while squeezed by the pressure of 610 kilometers of overlying rock (University of California, Santa Cruz 2013).

The two events ruptured differently. Zhan et al. (2014) found that the Okhotsk earthquake was mostly unilateral, rupturing about 90 kilometers along strike at more than 4 kilometers per second, while the Bolivia earthquake ruptured about half that distance at a slow velocity of about 1.5 kilometers per second and showed a major change in rupture direction. The difference matters because each candidate mechanism implies different behavior in rupture speed and extent. A fast, long rupture with a moderate stress drop resembles a shallow earthquake; Lay said of Okhotsk that it looks a lot like a shallow event (University of California, Santa Cruz 2013). The slow Bolivia rupture behaved differently, so no single description fits both.

sections.h: Mechanism One: Transformational Faulting
p: Olivine, the main mineral of the upper mantle, converts to denser structures as pressure rises. In old, cold slabs that reaction is kinetically hindered, so wedge-shaped zones of metastable olivine-bearing rock probably persist to depths of more than 600 kilometers (Kirby et al. 1996). Laboratory experiments on some metastable minerals show a shear instability called transformational faulting, in which the host mineral fails suddenly in thin shear zones where it transforms to a denser, finer-grained phase (Kirby et al. 1996). Green and Burnley (1989) observed this faulting in a germanium analogue of olivine, Mg2GeO4, and proposed that it arises from the generation, propagation and linking-up of small inclusions filled with the denser phase. Hasegawa and Nakajima (2017) describe the same idea in terms of small lens-shaped crystals of the new phase that grow and align along a plane until they form a fault.

Laboratory work supports the picture. Schubnel et al. (2013) recorded acoustic emissions resembling deep earthquakes in Mg2GeO4 olivine deformed at pressures of 4 to 5 gigapascals while it transformed, combining synchrotron X-ray measurements with acoustic monitoring (Wang et al. 2017). A 2022 study used natural (Mg,Fe)2SiO4 olivine at 11 to 17 gigapascals and 860 to 1350 kelvin, conditions equivalent to slabs in the transition zone. Through-going faulting occurred only within a narrow temperature window of 1100 to 1160 kelvin, accompanied by intense acoustic emissions at the onset of rupture. Fault sliding, aided by shear heating, occurred along a weak layer formed by the linking-up of lens-shaped packets of nanocrystalline olivine and wadsleyite (Ohuchi et al. 2022).

The hypothesis fits two observations: deep seismicity closely brackets the transition zone, and metastable olivine wedges are expected only in old, cold slabs (Kirby et al. 1996). It also faces objections. An early version, in which a sudden collapse of the mineral to a denser form produces the earthquake, would create a large isotropic, or implosive, component in the source, and deep earthquakes generally lack one (Hasegawa and Nakajima 2017). Silver et al. (1995) found that the Bolivia rupture extended at least 30 by 50 kilometers, more than three times the size expected for a metastable olivine wedge at the core of the slab, which they considered incompatible with an origin by transformational faulting.

sections.h: Mechanism Two: Dehydration Embrittlement
p: Subducting plates carry water-bearing minerals that break down as pressure and temperature rise. Under the dehydration embrittlement hypothesis, water expelled from these minerals generates earthquakes by raising the pore-fluid pressure in the rock. Hasegawa and Nakajima (2017) note that the details of how local excess pore pressure leads to rupture are still debated. They conclude that water from the slab plays an important role in generating intermediate-depth earthquakes, with rupture possibly starting through local excess pore pressure and then propagating through thermal shear instability.

Extending the idea below 300 kilometers is harder. The UC Santa Cruz release on the Okhotsk earthquake noted that fluid can lubricate a fault, but that all of the fluids should have been squeezed out of the slab before it reached that depth (University of California, Santa Cruz 2013). Zhang et al. (2021) nonetheless argue that dehydration embrittlement is a plausible alternative model for the Okhotsk event. Their argument rests on the orientation and size of the plane that ruptured, its rupture velocity and radiation efficiency, and diverse evidence that water is carried as deep as the transition zone and below. It is one of several competing interpretations of that earthquake.

sections.h: Mechanism Three: Thermal Runaway
p: The third hypothesis, thermal shear instability, starts with plastic deformation. If the rock deforms faster than the heat generated can escape, a positive feedback promotes further deformation. Deformation then proceeds rapidly until material in that part of the slab starts to melt, which produces sudden slip, that is, an earthquake (Hasegawa and Nakajima 2017).

Lay gave a similar description for Okhotsk: if the fault slips just a little, friction could melt the rock and provide the fluid, producing a runaway thermal effect. He added that something must first start the sliding (University of California, Santa Cruz 2013). Zhan et al. (2014) propose that this kind of shear melting operates inside warm slabs once a rupture has been triggered.

sections.h: Where Scientists Disagree
p: A review by Zhan (2020) reaches a plain conclusion about the three leading mechanisms. Transformational faulting, dehydration embrittlement and thermal runaway can each explain portions of the observations, and each has potentially fundamental difficulties explaining the rest. The review calls for more serious consideration of hypotheses that involve more than one mechanism: a deep earthquake might initiate by one process and propagate by another once triggered.

Comparison of the two largest events points the same way. Zhan et al. (2014) explain the differences between them as the result of two fundamentally different faulting mechanisms in slabs with different thermal states: transformational faulting inside the metastable olivine wedge in cold slab cores, and shear melting inside warm slabs once triggered. Lay noted that a transformation of mineral forms might give the initial kick, but that scientists cannot detect it directly (University of California, Santa Cruz 2013). That detection problem leaves the question of how ruptures begin open even where their propagation is better constrained.

Scale is another limit. The olivine samples in the 2022 experiments were 1.2 millimeters long (Ohuchi et al. 2022), while the Okhotsk rupture extended over many kilometers of fault. Researchers studying laboratory ruptures in millimeter-sized samples have noted that scaling issues between laboratory events and deep-focus earthquakes remain to be resolved (Wang et al. 2017). Each large deep event adds a constraint on slab temperature, mineral content and strength at depths no drill can reach. For readers watching a live earthquake feed, a large deep earthquake is therefore mainly a research opportunity, because the depth that makes it hard to explain also keeps most of its shaking far from the surface.

faq.q: What is a deep-focus earthquake?
faq.a: A deep-focus earthquake starts more than 300 kilometers below the surface, inside an oceanic plate that is sinking into the mantle. Earthquakes between about 70 and 300 kilometers are called intermediate-depth. The deepest earthquakes occur between about 325 and 690 kilometers, and activity ends abruptly near 700 kilometers.

faq.q: Why are deep earthquakes hard to explain?
faq.a: At depths beyond 100 to 200 kilometers, the pressure is so great that ordinary brittle fracture and frictional sliding would require unrealistic rock strengths. Rock at those depths would normally deform slowly instead of breaking, so some special mechanism must weaken the fault.

faq.q: What is the largest deep earthquake ever recorded?
faq.a: The magnitude 8.3 Sea of Okhotsk earthquake of 24 May 2013, about 600 kilometers deep. Its seismic moment was about 30 percent larger than that of the 1994 Bolivia earthquake, the previous record holder, and it released about three times as much energy.

faq.q: Are deep earthquakes dangerous?
faq.a: Deep earthquakes usually do not cause enough shaking at the surface to be hazardous, because the rupture lies hundreds of kilometers down.

faq.q: What are the main explanations for deep earthquakes?
faq.a: The three leading hypotheses are transformational faulting, where olivine that has stayed in its low-pressure form suddenly transforms along thin zones; dehydration embrittlement, where water released from minerals weakens the rock; and thermal runaway, where rapid deformation heats and melts a narrow zone. Each explains part of the observations.

faq.q: Do scientists agree on what causes deep earthquakes?
faq.a: No. A 2020 review concluded that each leading mechanism has potentially fundamental difficulties and suggested that a deep earthquake might start by one mechanism and continue by another. Studies of the 1994 Bolivia and 2013 Okhotsk events suggest that cold and warm slabs may fail in different ways.

title: Listening to Magma: How Volcanic Earthquakes, Tremor and Swarms Reveal Moving Fluids
description: How volcano-tectonic earthquakes, long-period events and tremor track magma and fluids, with Mount St. Helens 2004, Pinatubo 1991, Iliamna and Kilauea swarms.
dek: Volcanoes shake in ways ordinary faults do not. Cracking rock, resonating cracks and sustained tremor each tell observers something different about magma and gas on the move.
cardImage: a world map of recent M4.5+ earthquakes, with those on the Ring of Fire, the belt of ocean trenches and volcanoes around the Pacific, highlighted

sections.h: A Different Kind of Seismic Signal
p: Volcanoes produce a wider variety of seismic signals than ordinary fault zones do. Volcano-tectonic (VT) earthquakes were the first to be studied, because like tectonic earthquakes they are generated by brittle failure of rock (Konstantinou 2024). Long-period (LP) or hybrid earthquakes and volcanic tremor are generated through the complex interaction of fluids and gas with solid rock, which makes their source much harder to decipher (Konstantinou 2024). Chouet (1996) describes long-period seismicity as having typical periods of 0.2 to 2 seconds and as a reflection of pressure fluctuations caused by unsteady mass transport in the plumbing system beneath a volcano.

That distinction organizes the rest of this article. VT earthquakes and swarms tell observers that rock is cracking as magma or fluid pushes into new space. LP events and tremor suggest that fluid is moving inside cracks and conduits that already exist.

sections.h: Volcano-Tectonic Earthquakes and Swarms
p: White and McCausland (2016) compiled 136 VT earthquakes and swarms that preceded 111 eruptions at 83 volcanoes. They found that VT seismicity is usually the earliest reported seismic precursor at volcanoes that have been dormant for decades or more, and that it preceded all explosive eruptions of Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) 5 or larger in their data set. The activity tends to be swarm-like, begins days to years before an eruption, peaks at the time of the initial eruption, and has a large non-double-couple component in its focal mechanisms. The swarms usually start on tectonic faults one or two to tens of kilometers from the eventual vent rather than directly beneath it. The authors also show that the volume of intruded magma can be estimated from the cumulative seismic moment of the VT earthquakes (White and McCausland 2016).

Swarms can map the movement of magma even when no eruption follows. Two swarms beneath Iliamna Volcano in Alaska in May and August 1996 contained 88 and 2,833 locatable events, with magnitudes from -0.9 to 3.3. Their hypocenters formed a cluster in a previously aseismic volume of crust south of the summit, and increases in sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide emissions coincided with the second swarm. The authors explained the pattern by the emplacement and inflation of a subvertical dike. No eruption occurred (Roman et al. 2004).

On 23 August 2021, the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (HVO) reported a swarm beneath the south part of Kilauea's summit caldera. Early the next morning the swarm intensified, together with a faster rate of ground deformation at a nearby tiltmeter. HVO said these observations may indicate a small dike intrusion 1 to 2 kilometers beneath the south caldera. Over 100 earthquakes had been recorded by then, the largest of magnitude 3.3 and most below magnitude 1 (USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory 2021).

Interpretation is sometimes less direct. A magnitude 4.2 earthquake on 15 June 2020 on Unalaska Island, Alaska, began a sequence of hundreds of earthquakes at 7 to 10 kilometers depth, about 12 kilometers southeast of the summit of Makushin Volcano, and no eruptive activity or surface change was observed. Lanza et al. (2022) note that deciding whether such seismicity reflects magmatic or tectonic stresses is often challenging, although critical for hazard assessment. Their analysis found evidence of a local stress field likely induced by magma intrusion, and they conclude that the swarm was driven by a combination of magmatic and tectonic stresses.

sections.h: Long-Period Events: Resonating Cracks
p: A leading explanation for LP events is the resonance of a fluid-filled crack. In the model of Chouet (1988), a three-dimensional crack containing a viscous compressible fluid is set into resonance by an impulsive pressure transient applied over a small part of its surface, and a very slow wave trapped in the fluid, called the crack wave, sustains the vibration. The frequency, bandwidth and spacing of the resonant peaks depend strongly on the stiffness of the crack. In the same model, an LP event and harmonic tremor share the same source and differ in how the resonance is triggered and in the boundary conditions for fluid flow (Chouet 1988).

The model gives a way to read fluids from waveforms. Kumagai and Chouet (2000) estimated the quality factor, a measure of how slowly the vibration dies away, for a crack containing gas-gas mixtures, liquid-gas mixtures, and dusty or misty gases, and obtained values ranging from almost unity to several hundred. They suggest that changes in the complex frequencies of LP events could be interpreted in terms of changes in fluid composition beneath volcanoes.

Short, pulse-like LP events accompanied eruptive activity at Mount Etna in Italy in 2004 and 2008 and at Turrialba Volcano in Costa Rica and Ubinas Volcano in Peru in 2009. Chouet and Dawson (2016) found that a fluid-driven crack explains these pulses with realistic source sizes and fluid properties, and that the sources are shallow, less than 1 kilometer deep. A slow-rupture failure remains a possible alternative, though their synthetic waveforms fit the data less well under that model.

sections.h: Volcanic Tremor: A Sustained Signal With Several Candidate Sources
p: Tremor is a sustained vibration that can occur before or after eruptions and last from several minutes to several days or months. Its source can lie anywhere from a few hundred meters to 40 kilometers deep, depending on the volcano. Konstantinou and Schlindwein (2003) group the proposed sources into four families: fluid-flow-induced oscillations of conduits carrying magmatic fluids, resonance of fluid-filled cracks, bubble growth or collapse during hydrothermal boiling of groundwater, and oscillations of magma bodies. They note that many authors consider that the source of tremor is not unique and may differ from one volcano to another.

Julian (1994) described a nonlinear process analogous to the excitation of musical wind instruments and human vocal cords, in which fluid flowing through a channel with movable elastic walls produces oscillations. In that model, LP earthquakes appear when the magma flow rate is too low to sustain continuous tremor and a transient disturbance excites the channel instead. McNutt (2005) reports that tremor is stronger for fissure eruptions, phreatic eruptions and higher gas contents.

A study of noneruptive tremor on 2 October 2004 at Mount St. Helens offers a different view. Denlinger and Moran (2014) found that the signal was composed entirely of Love and Rayleigh waves and that the forces producing it were largely normal to the conduit walls. They concluded that the way tremor is generated masks the nature of its source, so that multiple models can explain the same signal and other data are needed to choose between them. With GPS and field data supporting rapid rise of magma, they inferred that this tremor resulted from the drag of nearly solid magma along rough conduit walls as it was forced toward the surface.

sections.h: Mount St. Helens, 2004: The Signals in Sequence
p: After 17 years and 11 months of quiet, Mount St. Helens began its reawakening on 23 September 2004 with a swarm of shallow VT earthquakes at depths of less than 2 kilometers. By 29 September, earthquakes of magnitude greater than 2 were occurring at about one per minute. A gradual transition from VT to hybrid and low-frequency events accompanied the intensification, a characteristic of many precursory swarms at the volcano before its dome-building eruptions in the 1980s. The first explosion occurred on 1 October, 8.5 days after the first earthquakes (Moran et al. 2008).

By 16 October the spacing between events had become so regular that the scientists called the earthquakes drumbeats, and these dominated seismicity through the end of 2005. Their size, spacing and spectra varied with changes in the style of extrusion at the surface but not with variations in magma flux, which suggests that drumbeat size and spacing depended more on the mechanics of extrusion than on the extrusion rate (Moran et al. 2008). Matoza and Chouet (2010) studied the smaller subevents that accompanied the drumbeats and concluded that the interaction of the hydrothermal and magmatic systems beneath the volcano could explain a wide range of observed phenomena, including subevents, LP events, larger events and phreatic explosions.

sections.h: Mount Pinatubo, 1991: Deep Long-Period Earthquakes
p: The vast majority of LP events reported in the literature originate at depths of less than 3 kilometers, but Mount Pinatubo produced something different. About 600 deep long-period earthquakes occurred beneath the volcano in late May and early June 1991, more than the combined total previously reported at all convergent-margin volcanoes worldwide (White 1996). White interprets them as the seismic expression of deep basaltic magma injected into the base of the magma chamber, which triggered the eruptive sequence. The onset of the deep activity on 26 May was followed just 1 hour later by shallow LP earthquakes and within 4 hours by continuous shallow tremor and a large steam emission (White 1996).

Seismic monitoring was the primary tool for assessing the evolving eruptive potential before the climactic eruption on 15 June. The team forecast the escalation from shifts in the locus of earthquake hypocenters, increases in total seismic energy release, changes in the character of the waveforms and growing nonseismic signs of unrest. The final days included a remarkable progression of increasingly large LP events from 12 to 14 June, followed by a 24-hour preclimactic period of high-amplitude, widely diverse seismic activity (Harlow et al. 1996).

sections.h: What Remains Unsettled
p: Volcano seismology supplies strong evidence that fluids are moving, but several questions stay open. McNutt (2005) notes that deep LP events are fairly common but may represent several processes. Tremor has competing source models, as the Mount St. Helens study shows. Swarms such as the one near Makushin can reflect magmatic and tectonic stress together, and a swarm can end without an eruption, as at Iliamna.

For readers who watch earthquake feeds, these examples offer a practical lesson. Many events in volcanic sequences are small, and their meaning often depends on other measurements, such as the tiltmeter record at Kilauea and the gas emissions at Iliamna. Seismic signals combined with deformation and gas data give observatories the best basis for judging whether magma is rising.

faq.q: What is a volcano-tectonic earthquake?
faq.a: A volcano-tectonic (VT) earthquake is caused by brittle failure of rock, like an ordinary tectonic earthquake, but it is driven by stresses from magma or fluids pushing into the crust near a volcano. VT swarms are usually the earliest seismic warning at volcanoes that have been dormant for decades.

faq.q: What are long-period volcanic earthquakes?
faq.a: Long-period (LP) events have typical periods of 0.2 to 2 seconds and are thought to come from pressure changes as magma, gas or steam moves through the volcano. A common model explains them as the resonance of a fluid-filled crack.

faq.q: What is volcanic tremor?
faq.a: Volcanic tremor is a sustained seismic signal near an active volcano that can last from minutes to days or months. Proposed sources include fluid flow through conduits, resonating cracks, boiling groundwater and oscillating magma bodies, and the source may differ from one volcano to another.

faq.q: Does an earthquake swarm under a volcano mean an eruption is coming?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Swarms at Iliamna in 1996 and near Makushin in 2020 ended without an eruption. Observatories combine earthquake data with ground deformation and gas measurements before judging whether magma is rising toward the surface.

faq.q: How did seismology help forecast the 1991 Pinatubo eruption?
faq.a: Scientists tracked shifts in where earthquakes occurred, the total seismic energy released and changes in waveforms. Deep long-period earthquakes from late May marked the arrival of new magma, and growing LP events from 12 to 14 June preceded the climactic eruption on 15 June.

faq.q: What were the drumbeat earthquakes at Mount St. Helens?
faq.a: During the 2004 to 2008 dome-building eruption, small earthquakes repeated at such regular intervals that scientists called them drumbeats. Their size and spacing changed with the style of lava extrusion rather than with the rate of magma supply.

title: Why Italy Shakes: The Apennines, L'Aquila and the Amatrice-Visso-Norcia Sequence
description: Why the Apennines produce normal-fault earthquakes: Adria, Tyrrhenian rollback, L'Aquila 2009, the 2016 Amatrice-Visso-Norcia sequence and deep CO2 fluids.
dek: Italy's deadliest recent earthquakes struck a mountain range that is being pulled apart. Here is what L'Aquila and the 2016 sequence revealed about the faults, the fluids and the open questions.
cardImage: an outline of Italy with the M6+ earthquakes of the Apennines since 1279 from the INGV CPTI15 catalogue, sized by magnitude, with Norcia 2016, L'Aquila 2009, Irpinia 1980 and Marsica 1915 labelled

sections.h: A Mountain Range Being Pulled Apart
p: The earthquakes that hit L'Aquila in 2009 and the Visso area in 2016 share a style that surprises many readers. Both occurred on normal faults, which accommodate stretching of the crust, in a mountain belt that was built by compression. The fault mechanisms of the 2016 sequence were consistent with extension of the central Apennines, which coexists with the opening of the Tyrrhenian back-arc basin (Gabrielli et al. 2022). Understanding why requires a look at the plate history beneath the peninsula.

Italy lies between two large plates and over a smaller one. Africa and Europe have been converging for a long time, and the Adriatic microplate, usually called Adria, is located between them. Le Breton et al. (2017) describe Adria as a key player in the geodynamics of the western Mediterranean, with highly deformed boundaries that include the Alps, the Apennines, the Dinarides, the Hellenides and the Calabrian Arc. The Apennines have been the site of Oligo-Miocene rollback subduction, a soft collision and pronounced back-arc extension (Le Breton et al. 2017).

Rollback is the central idea. A sinking slab retreats into the mantle, and the crust above it is stretched. Rosenbaum and Lister (2004) reconstructed the opening of the Tyrrhenian Sea and found that its major rifting began around 10 million years ago, in two episodes of back-arc extension induced by rollback of a west-dipping slab. The first period of extension, from 10 to 6 million years ago, was prominent in the northern Tyrrhenian Sea and the western part of the southern Tyrrhenian Sea, and the second mainly affected the southern Tyrrhenian Sea. They also identify a narrow slab beneath the Ionian Sea that underwent faster rollback and extreme rates of extension.

The consequence for earthquakes is a mountain belt that is stretching along its crest. Fonteijn et al. (2026) note that the central Apennines have experienced several destructive normal-faulting earthquakes in the last decade, and that fundamental questions persist about what drives the extension. Their modeling reproduces normal-faulting earthquakes, and horizontal surface velocities rising gradually to 3 millimeters per year, only when the slab beneath the central Apennines is detached. Le Breton et al. (2017) instead invoke crust-mantle decoupling, or delamination, during rollback in the Apennines. Rollback, delamination and a detached slab each have supporters, so the driver of extension remains contested.

sections.h: L'Aquila, April 2009
p: On 6 April 2009 at 01:32 UTC, a normal-faulting earthquake of Mw 6.1 struck the Abruzzo region. It caused 308 casualties and 70,000 evacuees and heavily damaged the city of L'Aquila and its cultural heritage (Chiaraluce 2012). Chiarabba et al. (2009) report the same event as Mw 6.3, a reminder that agencies can assign different moment magnitudes to one earthquake.

The mainshock began about 9.3 kilometers beneath L'Aquila and activated a fault about 16 kilometers long, trending northwest and dipping about 50 degrees to the southwest. A foreshock sequence that culminated in an Mw 4.0 event on 30 March had activated the same fault plane. Almost 3,000 events with a local magnitude of 1.9 or greater occurred in 2009, and the fault system reached about 40 kilometers in length by the end of December (Chiaraluce 2012). The aftershocks coincided with the surface trace of the Paganica fault, a poorly known normal fault before the event, and seismicity migrated northward onto an en echelon fault that could rupture in a future large earthquake (Chiarabba et al. 2009). Strong earthquakes had struck the same area in 1461 and 1703 (Chiaraluce 2010).

The fault system was more complex than a single plane. Seismicity nucleated within the upper 10 to 12 kilometers of the crust, and an Mw 5.4 event on 7 April nucleated a couple of kilometers deeper on a high-angle normal fault antithetic to the main system; its role is still unclear (Chiaraluce 2010). Another structure had a shallower dip of about 35 degrees that tends to flatten with depth, and the seismicity highlighted the activation of numerous minor normal fault segments within the whole system (Chiaraluce 2012).

sections.h: Amatrice, Visso and Norcia, 2016
p: The next major sequence began on 24 August 2016 with an Mw 6.0 earthquake near Amatrice that killed 299 people. An Mw 5.9 earthquake near Visso followed on 26 October, and an Mw 6.5 earthquake near Norcia on 30 October (Tan et al. 2021). The Visso earthquake therefore arrived two months after Amatrice, and Norcia four days after Visso. Together the three mainshocks activated an 80-kilometer normal-fault system (Tan et al. 2021). Between August and October 2016, 25,600 earthquakes from magnitude 0.1 to 6.5 were recorded, and digital networks installed immediately after Amatrice made it the best-monitored sequence to strike Italy. Eight events exceeded Mw 5.0 (Gabrielli et al. 2022). A machine-learning earthquake catalog showed that complex fault structures were activated during the sequence (Tan et al. 2021).

Older compressional structures influenced how the ruptures developed. Improta et al. (2019) used a high-quality catalog of early aftershocks to show that a lateral ramp of the Mount Sibillini thrust acted as a barrier for the Amatrice and Visso mainshocks and later as an asperity for the Norcia mainshock. A fault zone created by compression millions of years ago therefore helped decide where the extensional ruptures stopped and where they concentrated their slip.

sections.h: The Role of Deep Fluids
p: Many researchers think fluids helped drive the sequence. Gabrielli et al. (2022) conclude that fluids likely triggered the sequence and reduced the stability of the fault network after the Amatrice earthquake, with fluid migration nucleating the Visso and Norcia events. They attribute the spatial expansion of the affected area to deep migration of carbon-dioxide-bearing fluids from a source of trapped CO2 near Amatrice.

Other studies approach the question from different measurements. Convertito et al. (2020) modeled the delayed Visso events and found that Coulomb static stress transfer from the Amatrice earthquake did not instantaneously trigger the two large Visso aftershocks, whereas pore pressure diffusion initiated by the Amatrice deformation did. Convertito et al. also stress that anisotropic hydraulic conductivity must be included when computing pore pressure diffusion in this setting. Chiodini et al. (2020) assembled a 10-year record of tectonic CO2 flux in the Apennines and report massive emissions of deep CO2 coupled to the 2009 to 2018 Central Italy earthquakes. The studies point in the same direction, but Gabrielli et al. (2022) note that the spatial extent and mechanisms of fluid migration and diffusion through the fault network remain unclear.

sections.h: What Makes Italy Distinctive
p: Italy has an unusually long written record of its earthquakes. The Italian Macroseismic Database DBMI15, version 3.0, holds 123,956 macroseismic data points for 3,228 earthquakes and provides seismic histories for 15,332 localities, and an earlier release covered the years 1000 to 2017 (Istituto Nazionale di Geofisica e Vulcanologia 2021). The companion parametric catalogue, CPTI15, converts that evidence into locations and magnitudes for hazard assessment (Rovida et al. 2020). Few countries can compare a modern sequence with a thousand years of documented shaking.

The record shows a pattern of multiple mainshocks. Gabrielli et al. (2022) describe such sequences as common features of the Apennines, citing the 1980 Irpinia earthquake (Ms 6.9), the 1997 Umbria-Marche earthquake (Mw 6.0), the 2009 L'Aquila earthquake (Mw 6.1) and the 2016 sequence. Chiaraluce (2018) notes that mapping fault anatomy with small earthquakes of local magnitude above 0.5 helps characterize fault zone structure and its evolution, and that three sequences in 20 years (Colfiorito in 1997, L'Aquila in 2009 and Amatrice-Norcia-Visso in 2016 and 2017) activated a northwest-trending system of normal faults about 130 kilometers long. For readers watching a live feed, the 2016 sequence shows that a magnitude 6 earthquake in the Apennines can be followed within weeks or months by larger shocks on adjacent fault segments.

Three questions remain open: what drives the extension, how fluids move through the fault network, and why older thrusts act as barriers in some earthquakes and asperities in others. Each affects how future sequences are interpreted as they unfold.

faq.q: Why does Italy have so many earthquakes?
faq.a: Italy sits between the converging African and European plates, above the smaller Adriatic microplate (Adria). Rollback of a sinking slab opened the Tyrrhenian Sea and stretches the crust along the crest of the Apennines, and the destructive earthquakes of recent decades in the central Apennines have occurred on normal faults.

faq.q: What kind of faults caused the L'Aquila and Norcia earthquakes?
faq.a: Both were normal-fault earthquakes, which accommodate stretching of the crust. The fault mechanisms of the 2016 sequence were consistent with extension of the central Apennines, even though the mountain belt was originally built by compression.

faq.q: How strong was the 2009 L'Aquila earthquake?
faq.a: The 6 April 2009 earthquake had a moment magnitude of 6.1 in one study and 6.3 in another. It caused 308 casualties and 70,000 evacuees and heavily damaged the city of L'Aquila. Its aftershocks outlined the Paganica fault, a poorly known normal fault before the event.

faq.q: What happened in the 2016 Amatrice-Visso-Norcia sequence?
faq.a: An Mw 6.0 earthquake near Amatrice on 24 August 2016 killed 299 people. It was followed by an Mw 5.9 earthquake near Visso on 26 October and an Mw 6.5 earthquake near Norcia on 30 October. Together the three mainshocks activated an 80-kilometer normal-fault system.

faq.q: Did fluids trigger the 2016 earthquakes?
faq.a: Several studies point that way. One concludes that deep carbon-dioxide-bearing fluids likely triggered the sequence and helped nucleate the Visso and Norcia events, and another found that pore pressure diffusion, rather than static stress transfer, triggered the large Visso aftershocks. How fluids move through the fault network remains unclear.

faq.q: How far back does Italy's earthquake record go?
faq.a: The Italian Macroseismic Database DBMI15 holds 123,956 macroseismic data points for 3,228 earthquakes, and an earlier release covered the years 1000 to 2017. The companion catalogue CPTI15 turns that evidence into locations and magnitudes for hazard assessment.

title: Boxing Day 2004: The Sumatra-Andaman Earthquake and the Tsunami That Reached Phuket
description: How the 2004 Mw 9.1–9.3 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake made the tsunami that hit Phuket and Khao Lak: timing, wave heights, deaths and Thailand’s warning system.
dek: On 26 December 2004 a megathrust rupture off Sumatra lifted the seafloor and sent a tsunami across the Andaman Sea. In Phuket the sea drew back first. Here is what happened, and what changed.
cardImage: an outline map of Thailand with Phuket and Phang Nga provinces highlighted, the USGS epicentre of the M9.1 earthquake off northern Sumatra, and a dashed line to Phuket marking the tsunami's travel time of about 100 minutes; Khao Lak, Banda Aceh and Bangkok are labelled

sections.h: The Earthquake Beneath the Andaman Sea
p: At 00:58:53 UTC on 26 December 2004, a megathrust earthquake struck off the west coast of northern Sumatra. Thailand is seven hours ahead of UTC, so the time in Phuket was close to 8 a.m., on the morning after Christmas (Ioualalen et al. 2007). The U.S. Geological Survey describes a magnitude 9.1 earthquake in which the India Plate, an oceanic plate, is subducted beneath the Burma microplate, part of the larger Sunda plate, with the boundary marked by the Sunda Trench. The rupture occurred on the interplate thrust with very little oblique motion (U.S. Geological Survey n.d.).

The magnitude took months to settle. The first estimate of 9.0 came from surface waves. Stein and Okal (2005) analyzed the normal modes of the whole planet and reported a seismic moment 2.5 times larger than initial reports suggested, equivalent to Mw 9.3 and second only to the 1960 Chile earthquake. Lay et al. (2005) gave a range of Mw 9.1 to 9.3. The size therefore depends on the waves and periods used to measure it, and the published range remains 9.1 to 9.3.

The fault break was enormous. Science News (2005) reports a rupture 1,200 to 1,300 kilometers long. In the first minute the rupture front advanced northwest at about 500 meters per second, then accelerated to about 3 kilometers per second for four minutes, and then slowed but continued north for another six minutes. Slip varied along the rupture. Lay et al. (2005) report up to 15 meters of slip near Banda Aceh and much smaller, rapid slip farther north along the Nicobar and Andaman Islands, while the tsunami model of Ioualalen et al. (2007) uses slip of 12 to 18 meters with a maximum of about 23 meters. Estimates of peak slip therefore differ between studies. Shearer and Bürgmann (2010) add that convergence rates are relatively slow along this margin, particularly in the northern part of the rupture zone.

sections.h: How the Seafloor Became a Wave
p: Science News (2005) explains the setup: decades of tectonic motion before the earthquake had dragged the seafloor west of Sumatra below its normal, unflexed position, and the rupture released it. Ioualalen et al. (2007) modeled about 9 to 10 meters of uplift on the western side of the trench and about 5 meters of subsidence on the eastern side. Papadopoulos et al. (2006) found that the tsunami propagated as a leading crest to the west, in Sri Lanka and the Maldives, and as a leading trough to the east, in Thailand. People on Thai beaches therefore saw the sea retreat before they saw it rise.

sections.h: Phuket on the Morning of 26 December
p: Thailand lies about 500 kilometers east of the source (Tsuji et al. 2006). The tsunami reached Phuket Island about 100 minutes after the earthquake, which places its arrival near 9:40 a.m. local time, during high tide and with a leading depression wave (Szczuciński et al. 2012). Seven tide gauge records from the Thai coast all show the sea level withdrawing first for 30 to 60 minutes, followed by a rise, which matches survivors' accounts (Tsuji et al. 2006).

Eyewitnesses described two major waves about 40 minutes apart, with the second generally reported as the larger, and some reported up to seven waves in total (Szczuciński et al. 2012). The withdrawal was a warning sign, and Ioualalen et al. (2007) note that this crucial sign was often misread. Several waves in the sequence arrived without a retreat between them, and the wavefront speed at Phuket was estimated at 14.4 kilometers per hour (Szczuciński et al. 2012).

Wave heights varied sharply along the coast. Field teams measured tsunami heights above 5 meters on Phuket Island and above 10 meters at Khao Lak, about 50 kilometers to the north (Tsuji et al. 2006). Ioualalen et al. (2007) compiled observed runups at 58 Thai locations ranging from 1.47 to 11.29 meters with a mean of 6.11 meters, and they report the largest runups of 11 to 14 meters near Khao Lak. Their simulation reproduced the observed runups with a correlation of 0.92, including the strong variation along the coast, which supports the source model they used. Szczuciński et al. (2012) found that runup on their Phuket transects was below 6 meters and that measured wave heights exceeded 15 meters at Pakarang Cape in Phang Nga. A reef offshore of Kho Khao Island held runup below 3 meters along the part of the coast it protected, while nearby unprotected sectors exceeded 6 meters (Szczuciński et al. 2012). The Tsuji survey found the highest tsunami height, 19.6 meters, at Ban Thung Dap on Phra Thong Island (Tsuji et al. 2006).

The water also moved sediment inland. Tsunami deposits reached up to about 1.5 kilometers from the shore, reached up to about 40 centimeters in thickness, and were mostly under 10 centimeters thick (Szczuciński et al. 2012).

sections.h: Lives Lost and Contested Counts
p: Phuket recorded 259 confirmed deaths, and hundreds of people remain unaccounted for (Thaiger 2024). Phang Nga province to the north suffered far more: Ioualalen et al. (2007) report 8,500 people dead or missing in Thailand, with Phang Nga accounting for 71 percent. They note that Phuket's share is given as 5 percent in one place and 9 percent in another in the same source, so the Phuket fraction of that total is uncertain.

The regional toll also varies by source. Lay et al. (2005) state that the tsunami caused more than 283,000 deaths. Other published tallies are lower, near 226,000 (Japan Times 2017), and Thai figures separate confirmed deaths from missing people, as the Phuket counts show. A single death toll for 2004 should therefore be read as an estimate.

sections.h: Why There Was No Warning
p: There was no tsunami warning system in the Indian Ocean in 2004, although experts had recommended one. When the earthquake was detected, some time elapsed before its tsunami potential could be assessed (National Research Council 2006). Staff at the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center in Hawaii said they tried to warn Indian Ocean nations but lacked the equipment to monitor that part of the world and the phone numbers of the right officials (NBC News 2005). Before 2004 only six deep-ocean tsunami buoys were in place worldwide (NOAA Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory n.d.). Australia, Chile, Indonesia and Thailand have since deployed such buoys as part of their warning systems (NOAA Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory n.d.).

Thai forecasters had a precedent. Smith Thammasaroj, then head of Thailand's meteorological department, was accused of scare-mongering in 1998 when he warned that the southwest coast could face a deadly tsunami (NBC News 2005).

sections.h: What Changed
p: Thailand built a National Disaster Warning Center. By 2007 it had 79 warning towers in coastal provinces and a deep-sea buoy in the Indian Ocean, although the center's lines of authority were still unclear (The New Humanitarian 2007). In 2017 the deputy director-general of Thailand's disaster prevention department said that up to 80 percent of the warning system needed maintenance (Japan Times 2017). Twenty years after the event, activists in Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia reported that early warning systems and buoys are in place, while public awareness is lacking. Malaysia's meteorological department established a National Tsunami Early Warning System that is integrated with systems including the U.S.-run Pacific Tsunami Warning Center in Hawaii (Radio Free Asia 2024).

faq.q: What caused the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami?
faq.a: A megathrust earthquake on 26 December 2004 off the west coast of northern Sumatra, where the India Plate is subducted beneath the Burma microplate. The rupture released seafloor that had been dragged down for decades, lifting it by about 9 to 10 meters west of the trench and lowering it by about 5 meters to the east.

faq.q: How strong was the 2004 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake?
faq.a: The U.S. Geological Survey gives magnitude 9.1. Analysis of the whole Earth's normal modes gave Mw 9.3, and other studies give 9.1 to 9.3, so the published range remains 9.1 to 9.3. The rupture was 1,200 to 1,300 kilometers long.

faq.q: When did the tsunami reach Phuket?
faq.a: About 100 minutes after the earthquake, near 9:40 a.m. local time. Tide gauges on the Thai coast show the sea withdrawing first for 30 to 60 minutes before it rose, and eyewitnesses described two major waves about 40 minutes apart.

faq.q: Why did the sea go out before the tsunami hit Thailand?
faq.a: The tsunami travelled east as a leading trough, because the seafloor on the eastern side of the rupture dropped. On Thai beaches the sea therefore retreated before it rose. This warning sign was often misread.

faq.q: How high was the tsunami in Phuket and Khao Lak?
faq.a: Field surveys measured tsunami heights above 5 meters on Phuket Island and above 10 meters at Khao Lak, with the largest runups of 11 to 14 meters near Khao Lak and a highest tsunami height of 19.6 meters on Phra Thong Island.

faq.q: Does Thailand have a tsunami warning system now?
faq.a: Yes. Thailand built a National Disaster Warning Center, which by 2007 had 79 warning towers in coastal provinces and a deep-sea buoy in the Indian Ocean. In 2017 officials said up to 80 percent of the system needed maintenance, and activists in 2024 said public awareness is still lacking.
